result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn 'validate' into a narrower decision and warn that stated interest doesn't predict purchase. A's plan fits the time available better: 5–6 owner calls, 2–3 sitter calls, one mock screen within the designer's 3 hours a week, findings reported as 'n of N', and a clear list of what the user must do personally. B packs 8–10 owner calls, 3–4 sitter calls and an engineering fake-door test into two weeks, uses an example take-rate threshold ('above 5%') that reads like a made-up benchmark, and never sets out the human-only steps as clearly as A. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B fits the real limits better. It keeps the designer to 3 hours a week, leaves the fake door as a next step after legal review instead of squeezing an engineering build into two weeks, and lists plainly which steps the PM must do. It also warns against percentages at this sample size. A has good thinking on the decision and on feasibility, but its 5% take-rate threshold reads like an invented benchmark, its designer-hour sums are muddled, and it never clearly says which tasks a human has to do.
